LONDON, England (CNN) -- What recession? Christie's, the famed auction house, this week sold a nearly 36-carat diamond for $24.3 million, which it said was the highest price for a diamond sold at auction. The 35.56-carat diamond dates back to the 17th century. The previous record was a mere $16.5 million for a 100-carat diamond in 1995, Christie's said. "In the midst of these challenging times, we were thrilled to achieve an historic price for an historic diamond," said Francois Curiel, chairman of Christie's Europe and auctioneer for Wednesday's sale. The 35.56-carat Wittelsbach blue diamond, dating to the 17th century, was purchased by international jeweler Laurence Graff, the auction house said in a release. Graff was bidding against Aleks Paul of Essex Global Trading, a professional of Russian origin based in New York, Christie's said. "Known as 'Der Blaue Wittelsbacher' since 1722, it is one of very few diamonds which can claim 17th century heritage, incredible rarity and exceptional beauty." The diamond, mined in India nearly 400 years ago, has been privately owned since 1964. Until 1723, Christie's said, all diamonds worn by European royalty came from India. The diamond has a royal lineage. Christie's traces it thus: King Philip IV of Spain (1605-1665) selected the diamond in 1664 as part of a dowry for his daughter, the Infanta Margarita Teresa (1651-1673). She had become engaged to Leopold I of Austria (1640-1705), who later became Holy Roman Emperor. When she died in 1673, her husband retained the diamond, which was passed on to his heirs. In 1722, the diamond entered the Wittelsbach family when the Archduchess Maria Amalia of Austria (1701-1756) married the Bavarian Crown Prince, Charles Albert (1697-1745). It was worn by successive rulers until the abdication of King Ludwig III (1845-1921) in 1918. The world's largest deep blue diamond is the "Hope Diamond," a 45.52-carat stone housed at the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, DC. Diamonds apparently are recession-proof. Christie's reported jewelry sales of $226 million for the first half of 2008, calling it "the best jewelry season ever seen at auction." Sales for the first six months of this year marked a 32 percent increase over the same period in 2007, Christie's said. According to Christie's, key diamonds the company sold in the first half of 2008 included a 13.39-carat fancy intense blue diamond that fetched $8.9 million in Geneva on May 14 and the pear-shaped potentially flawless 38-carat Onassis diamond, which sold for $7.1 million on June 11 in London.

# Rare blue diamond sells for record $24.3 million in London

**LONDON** — A 35.56-carat blue diamond with centuries of royal history sold for $24.3 million at Christie’s in London, setting a world auction record for any diamond or jewel despite a deepening global recession.

The Wittelsbach Diamond fetched £16.4 million Wednesday, far exceeding its presale estimate of about £9 million. London jeweler Laurence Graff won the stone after several minutes of bidding, Christie’s said.

The cushion-shaped, deep grayish-blue diamond is one of the world’s most celebrated historic gems. Believed to have originated in India, it first appeared in European royal records in the 17th century and was associated with Margarita Teresa, daughter of Spain’s King Philip IV.

The diamond later passed into the Austrian imperial family before reaching Bavaria’s ruling Wittelsbach dynasty through marriage. It became part of the Bavarian crown jewels and was displayed in the royal crown in the 19th century. After the monarchy fell, the stone disappeared from public view for decades and eventually entered a private collection.

Its combination of size, color, rarity and royal provenance helped drive the price to a record, auction officials said. Blue diamonds are among the rarest colored diamonds, with only a small number of large examples known to exist.

The sale came at an unlikely moment for the luxury market. The global financial crisis had battered stock markets, weakened consumer confidence and forced many shoppers to cut discretionary spending. High-end retailers were reporting slower sales, while auction houses faced a more selective group of buyers.

Yet the Wittelsbach’s result suggested that exceptional stones could remain insulated from the broader downturn. Wealthy collectors have often treated rare diamonds as portable stores of value, particularly when financial markets are volatile.

The market was far from uniformly strong, however. More ordinary jewelry and pieces carrying aggressive estimates faced greater difficulty as buyers became cautious. Auction specialists said demand during the recession was concentrating on objects with impeccable provenance, scarcity and long-term investment appeal.

Graff said the diamond ranked among the most important stones he had seen in his career. Its $24.3 million price surpassed the previous auction record for a diamond, held by a 100.10-carat colorless stone sold in Geneva in 1995.

For Christie’s, the sale offered a dramatic reminder that even during one of the worst economic downturns in decades, a gem tied to European royalty could still inspire fierce competition — and a record-setting bid.

counterfactuals.output:
## Sale of the Wittelsbach Blue Diamond

The 35.56-carat Wittelsbach Blue was sold by Christie’s in London on 10 December 2008 to British billionaire jeweller **Laurence Graff**.

- **Price including buyer’s premium:** **£16,393,250**, approximately **US$24.3 million**
- **Hammer price:** about **£14.6 million**
- **Pre-sale estimate:** roughly **£9 million**

Graff subsequently had the stone recut to remove chips and improve its colour and clarity, reducing it to 31.06 carats, and renamed it the **Wittelsbach-Graff Diamond**.

### Provenance

The deep blue diamond is believed to have originated in the **Golconda mines of India**, the source of several celebrated historic diamonds. Its early history is partly traditional rather than conclusively documented.

It is commonly said to have belonged to **King Philip IV of Spain**, who gave it to his daughter, **Infanta Margarita Teresa**, in connection with her 1666 marriage to the Habsburg emperor **Leopold I**. It subsequently entered the Austrian imperial collection.

In 1722, the diamond passed into the Bavarian **House of Wittelsbach**, traditionally associated with the marriage of Archduchess Maria Amalia of Austria to the future Holy Roman Emperor Charles VII. When Bavaria became a kingdom in 1806, the stone was mounted in the Bavarian royal crown and became one of the family’s principal crown jewels.

After the fall of the Bavarian monarchy in 1918, it remained with the Wittelsbach family. It was offered at Christie’s in 1931 but failed to sell, was later disposed of privately, and eventually entered another private collection before returning to Christie’s in 2008.

### Comparison with earlier auction records

The 2008 price established a new auction record at the time for:

- **Any diamond sold at auction**
- **Any jewel sold at auction**

The previous record was about **US$16.5 million**, paid at Sotheby’s Geneva in 1995 for the **100.10-carat “Star of the Season,”** a colourless pear-shaped diamond. At approximately **US$24.3 million**, the Wittelsbach Blue exceeded that record by nearly **US$8 million**, or about **47%**.

Its price worked out to approximately **US$684,000 per carat**. The sale was especially notable because the Wittelsbach was valued not only for its rare natural blue colour but also for its royal history and close gemological resemblance to the Hope Diamond.

counterfactuals.output:
# Diamonds Look “Recession-Proof” as Christie’s 2008 Sales Shine

**LONDON —** Global markets plunged, banks failed and consumers sharply curtailed spending in 2008. Yet at the top end of the jewelry market, collectors continued to pay extraordinary prices for exceptional diamonds—culminating in the record-setting sale of a blue gem with a history stretching back to 17th-century European royalty.

Christie’s reported worldwide jewelry sales of approximately **$430 million in 2008**, a result that underscored the resilience of rare stones and signed jewels during one of the worst financial crises in decades. The year’s defining moment came in December, when the auction house sold the **Wittelsbach Diamond**, a 35.56-carat historic blue diamond, for **£16.4 million, or about $24.3 million**.

London jeweler Laurence Graff bought the stone after a closely watched competition at Christie’s in London. The price was more than double its presale estimate and, at the time, established a world auction record for any diamond or jewel.

The sale offered dramatic evidence for an idea frequently repeated in auction rooms: that the rarest diamonds can be “recession-proof.” As stock markets lost trillions of dollars in value and the collapse of Lehman Brothers intensified the global credit crisis, bidders still competed for an object whose combination of color, size, provenance and scarcity could not easily be replicated.

## A Diamond With a Royal History

The Wittelsbach is believed to have originated in India’s Golconda region, the source of some of history’s most celebrated diamonds. Its European history dates to the 17th century, when the stone was associated with the Habsburg court.

It entered the Austrian royal family through the marriage of **Infanta Margarita Teresa of Spain to Emperor Leopold I**. The diamond later passed to their daughter, Maria Antonia, and eventually became part of the Bavarian crown jewels after entering the House of Wittelsbach, the dynasty from which it took its modern name.

The gem was mounted in successive royal ornaments and appeared in a Bavarian crown before disappearing from public view during the 20th century. Its return to auction therefore attracted not only diamond buyers but also collectors of royal and European historical objects.

Christie’s described the stone as a fancy deep grayish-blue diamond. Although it differed in tone and clarity from modern expectations of a flawless blue gem, its historical significance and remarkable size made direct comparisons difficult. Natural blue diamonds are among the rarest colored diamonds, their hue generally produced by trace amounts of boron within the crystal structure.

## Strength at the Very Top

The Wittelsbach sale was exceptional, but it was not an isolated bright spot. Christie’s jewelry auctions in Geneva, New York, London and Hong Kong continued to draw international buyers throughout 2008, helping the department produce one of its strongest annual performances.

Demand was concentrated in a few categories: large white diamonds, vivid colored diamonds, untreated colored gemstones, signed pieces by major houses and jewels with aristocratic or celebrity provenance. Buyers from established markets in Europe and the United States faced increasing competition from collectors in Russia, the Middle East and Asia.

That international depth helped support prices even as the economic outlook deteriorated. Wealthy collectors could bid in several currencies and often viewed major stones as portable, internationally recognized stores of value. Unlike shares in a company or certain financial instruments, a historic diamond is a tangible object whose supply cannot be expanded in response to demand.

Auction houses also benefited from rarity. Owners of important jewels often hold them for decades, meaning that a major blue diamond or royal jewel may appear only once in a generation. When one reaches the market, collectors cannot assume that a similar example will soon follow.

## “Recession-Proof”—But Only to a Point

The results do not mean the entire diamond industry escaped the downturn. The financial crisis hurt retail jewelers, diamond manufacturers and mining companies as credit tightened and consumers postponed discretionary purchases. Commercial-grade stones, modern jewelry without notable provenance and goods dependent on middle-income spending faced substantially greater pressure.

Even within auctions, success was selective. Buyers favored exceptional quality and were less forgiving of optimistic estimates or ordinary material. In that sense, 2008 did not prove that every diamond was recession-proof. It suggested instead that the world’s rarest and most historically important gems could behave differently from the broader luxury market.

The Wittelsbach’s price also reflected factors beyond carat weight. Its royal lineage, centuries-old history, blue color and long absence from public sale gave it the qualities of both a jewel and a cultural artifact. A more common diamond of similar size would not necessarily inspire the same competition.

Still, the timing was striking. The stone crossed the auction block only months after the failure of major financial institutions and amid mounting fears of a worldwide recession. Rather than depressing the price, the crisis coincided with a bidding contest that drove the diamond far above expectations.

For Christie’s, the result provided a glittering conclusion to a turbulent year. For collectors, it reinforced a longstanding conviction: financial assets may rise and fall, but a truly irreplaceable diamond—especially one with royal bloodlines—can retain its allure even when confidence elsewhere is in short supply.

“Der Blaue Wittelsbacher” (“the Blue Wittelsbach”), a rare deep-blue diamond probably mined in India, first appears in European royal records in the 17th century.

- **Spanish Habsburgs:** King **Philip IV of Spain** acquired the 35.56-carat stone and included it in the dowry of his daughter, **Infanta Margarita Teresa**, for her 1666 marriage to **Emperor Leopold I**.
- **Austrian Habsburgs:** After Margarita Teresa’s death, the diamond remained within the imperial family and passed to their daughter, **Archduchess Maria Antonia of Austria**.
- **Bavarian Wittelsbachs:** Maria Antonia married **Maximilian II Emanuel, Elector of Bavaria**, bringing the diamond into the Wittelsbach dynasty. It was recorded among the Bavarian jewels in 1722, was displayed in insignia of the Order of the Golden Fleece, and later became part of the Bavarian crown jewels after Bavaria became a kingdom in 1806.
- **After the monarchy:** Following the fall of the Bavarian monarchy in 1918, the stone was assigned to the Wittelsbach family’s compensation fund. It was offered at Christie’s in 1931 but failed to sell, then passed through dealers and private owners before resurfacing publicly in the 1960s.

On **10 December 2008**, Christie’s London auctioned the diamond for **£16.39 million—about US$24.3 million—to jeweler Laurence Graff**. The price far exceeded its estimate and set the then-world auction record for any diamond or jewel.

Graff subsequently had the stone recut—controversially—to improve its clarity, reducing it from **35.56 to 31.06 carats**, and renamed it the **Wittelsbach-Graff Diamond**. It was later exhibited beside the Hope Diamond at the Smithsonian.

**LONDON, England (CNN)** — The Wittelsbach Diamond, a rare blue gem weighing nearly 36 carats, sold at Christie’s in London for £16.4 million ($24.3 million) Wednesday, setting what the auction house said was a world record for any diamond or jewel sold at auction.

London jeweler Laurence Graff bought the 35.56-carat stone after roughly 15 minutes of bidding. The contest began at about £3 million and narrowed to Graff and a telephone bidder before the hammer fell at £14.6 million. Fees brought the final price to £16,393,250.

Christie’s called the result “a world record price for any diamond and any jewel sold at auction.” The diamond had been expected to fetch at least £9 million.

François Curiel, chairman of Christie’s Europe and its international jewelry department, described the sale as a historic moment and said the auction house was honored to have handled one of the world’s best-known diamonds.

The deep grayish-blue, cushion-shaped stone has often been compared with the Hope Diamond, the 45.52-carat blue gem held by the Smithsonian Institution in Washington. Both are believed to have originated in India’s Golconda region and share unusually similar coloring, although researchers have not established that they were cut from the same original stone.

The Wittelsbach’s documented history stretches back to the 17th century. It passed through European royal families and became part of the Bavarian crown jewels after entering the House of Wittelsbach through marriage.

The sale eclipsed the previous auction record for a jewel: $16.5 million paid in 1995 for the 100.10-carat “Star of the Season” diamond. It also capped a strong 2008 for rare blue stones. In May, Christie’s Geneva sold a 13.39-carat blue diamond for about $8.9 million.

Graff said he intended to examine the Wittelsbach carefully before deciding how best to preserve and present the historic gem.
